claim: Prefers adaptive attacks written against the specific, fully specified defense over testing against previously known fixed attacks because a defense can trivially 'defeat' a fixed attack without being any more secure.
quote: a defense is only interesting from the perspective of a security evaluation if it withstands future attack. Showing that a defense can defeat previous attacks is a necessary, but not sufficient, component of an evaluation.
title: Advice on Evaluating Adversarial Example Defenses

claim: Prefers asking 'what attack could possibly defeat this?' and showing every plausible attack fails over demonstrating success on a convenient benchmark, because the evaluator's job is to try to break the system.
quote: After the defense has been defined, ask: what attack could possibly defeat this defense? All attacks that might work must be shown to be ineffective.
title: Advice on Evaluating Adversarial Example Defenses

claim: Prefers threat models that do not constrain the adversary's approach over arbitrary limits on attacker effort because there is no realistic reason an attacker could do 100 steps but not 1000.
quote: There is no reasonable threat model under which an attacker can compute 10 (or 100) iterations of gradient descent, but not 1000. Because the threat model must not constrain the approach an attacker takes, it is always worth evaluating against a strong attack
title: Advice on Evaluating Adversarial Example Defenses

claim: Distrusts evaluations using weak or non-adaptive attacks (e.g., FGS only) because they can be passed via artifacts like gradient masking and give a false sense of robustness.
quote: It was never intended to be a strong attack for evaluating the robustness of a neural network, and should not be used as one.
title: Advice on Evaluating Adversarial Example Defenses

claim: Uses internal-consistency sanity checks (iterative >= single-step, white-box >= black-box, monotonic in distortion, unbounded reaches 100%) to detect a flawed evaluation; violations signal a bug in the test rather than a real finding.
quote: Iterative attacks are strictly more powerful than single-step attacks, and so their results should be strictly superior. If an iterative attack performs worse than a single-step attack, this often indicates that the iterative attack is not correct.
title: Advice on Evaluating Adversarial Example Defenses

claim: prefers evaluation against adaptive adversaries who know the specifics of the defense over non-adaptive or zero-knowledge tests because passing weak tests says almost nothing about real-world robustness.
quote: Defending against non-adaptive attacks is necessary but not sufficient. It is our firm belief that an evaluation against non-adaptive attacks is of very limited utility.
title: On Evaluating Adversarial Robustness

claim: prefers applying the mindset of a future real adversary over running off-the-shelf tests with default settings because defaults are tuned to past setups and can silently fail on a new target.
quote: applying the same mindset that a future adversary would apply is the only way to show that a defense might be able to withstand the test of time.
title: On Evaluating Adversarial Robustness

claim: Distrusts a negative result (attack fails, defense looks robust) because it may reflect a flawed or poorly tuned test rather than true robustness, so failure to elicit a behavior is weak evidence.
quote: gradient masking may make optimization-based attacks fail but that does not mean that the space of adversarial perturbations decreased.
title: On Evaluating Adversarial Robustness

claim: Validate your test harness itself by checking it succeeds on known-broken or intentionally-vulnerable targets, so that a null result is interpretable.
quote: This can be done by selecting alternate models that are either known to be insecure or are intentionally designed to be insecure, and verify that the new attack algorithm can effectively break these defenses.
title: On Evaluating Adversarial Robustness

claim: Prefers actively planting a known ground-truth positive (an injected adversarial example) over passively observing that an attack fails, because failure alone cannot distinguish a robust model from a weak attack.
quote: Our test purposefully injects adversarial examples into a defense and then checks if the attack used to evaluate the defense is able to find them. If the attack fails this test, we know that the attack is too weak
title: Increasing Confidence in Adversarial Robustness Evaluations

claim: Prefers treating a null result as uninformative unless the evaluator proves the instrument could have detected the effect, because absence of a finding is ambiguous between true robustness and weak probing.
quote: There are two reasons an attack might not find an adversarial example. Either the classifier is robust or the attack is too weak and it could not find the existing adversarials.
title: Increasing Confidence in Adversarial Robustness Evaluations

claim: Calibrate the difficulty of a test against a trivial baseline (random attack) and start from the hardest setting, because a test that is too easy has no predictive power and one too hard underestimates real ability.
quote: a test that is too easy has no predictive power about the attack’s efficacy (since any attack might trivially pass it), while on the other hand, a test that is too challenging might actually underestimate the attack’s true performance
title: Increasing Confidence in Adversarial Robustness Evaluations

claim: prefers validating an evaluation against test cases with known, constructed-by-brute-force positive answers over trusting a failed attack as evidence of robustness because a failure may just reflect a weak attack.
quote: first, we construct test cases with known adversarial examples that we have identified a priori; then, we run the attack on these test cases and verify they succeed.
title: Are aligned neural networks adversarially aligned?

claim: Distrusts the inference 'our attacks/evals did not find the behavior, therefore the model is safe', since absence of elicitation may reflect an insufficiently powerful probe.
quote: the failure of current attacks should not be seen as proof that aligned text models remain aligned under adversarial inputs.
title: Are aligned neural networks adversarially aligned?

claim: prefers evaluation tests where existence of a solution is guaranteed by construction over open-ended tests because then any failure unambiguously indicates a flawed tool.
quote: Observe that a sufficiently strong attack (e.g. a brute force search over all prompts) will always succeed on this test: any failure thus indicates a flawed attack.
title: Are aligned neural networks adversarially aligned?

claim: In a setup, respect the real deployment format (fixed chat template, attacker controls only the user turn, prior history unmodifiable) instead of giving the adversary unrealistic control over the prompt because unrealistic control makes the result irrelevant to real deployments.
quote: the attacker controls the tokens right before the model’s generation, which makes an attack much easier (but not relevant for current chat bot deployments).
title: Are aligned neural networks adversarially aligned?

claim: prefers tests drawn from tasks actually asked in real usage over academic homework-style questions because what matters is whether models do what users really need.
quote: Existing benchmarks tend to focus on solving typical problems that might be assigned to a student as homework. But the types of questions that are assigned to students are different from the types of questions I want to ask a language model to solve for me.
title: My benchmark for large language models

claim: In a setup, extract the essence of a real, context-specific task and rewrite it as a question instead of inventing synthetic scenarios, because realism comes from situations actually encountered.
quote: Or, in cases where the actual task I was asking for is context-specific and impossible to evaluate automatically, I've tried to extract the essence of the task and write a correspodning question.
title: My benchmark for large language models

claim: In a setup, use plain, unpolished natural prompts the way a lazy real user would instead of engineered prompting tricks, because heavily engineered prompts don't reflect how models are really used and signal a test.
quote: I do not want to remind the model it is AN EXPERT IN PYTHON and tell it that I'll give it a $100,000 tip for giving the right answer OR I WILL MURDER A KITTEN but please pause....take a deep breath....and think step by step by step before answering.
title: My benchmark for large language models

claim: Give the model a live tool-like environment (e.g., a real SQL database or terminal looped with its outputs) and observe multi-step behavior, since this reveals capabilities that single-shot Q&A hides.
quote: In this test, I directly connect the model up to a SQL database, piping any model output directly to the database, and any output back to the model.
title: My benchmark for large language models

claim: prefers evaluating a defense against an attack built specifically for it over a generic benchmark because the only attack that matters is the one tailored to break that specific defense.
quote: There is no single benchmark for security. You can't just evaluate your defense on “the attack benchmark” and call it a day. Because the only attack that matters is the one that's designed to break your specific defense.
title: Why I attack

claim: Understand the system better than its builder to find exploits; deep system knowledge, not generic probing, is what surfaces real failures.
quote: The only way you'll come up with an exploit is by understanding the system better than the person who built it in the first place! Because they (presumably) aren't aware of any exploits
title: Why I attack

claim: Prefers a realistic, fully scaffolded agent environment with tool use over simplified simulated environments judged by LLMs, because rigorous measurement of attack success needs real-world-like interaction.
quote: Rigor ously evaluating the effectiveness of prompt injection attacks and defenses necessitates a realistic AI agent environment that closely mimics real-world scenarios. Such an environment should include comprehensive system scaffolding with tool use, enabling the simulation of complex interactions.
title: Position: Adversarial ML for LLMs Is Not Making Any Progress

claim: Distrusts evaluations that simulate environments for simplicity and rely on LLM judges, since they trade rigor for convenience and make outcomes less precisely measurable.
quote: However, for simplicity, many studies opt to simulate these environments and rely on LLMs as judges for evaluation. There are new setups that have more rigorous evaluations (Debenedetti et al., 2024), where the attack's success and utility can be precisely measured
title: Position: Adversarial ML for LLMs Is Not Making Any Progress

claim: Prefers outcomes that can be directly and objectively measured (e.g., an unauthorized action actually taken) over subjective judgments of text, because clear success criteria make evidence convincing.
quote: The primary goal of prompt injections is often clear— for instance, manipulating a language model to perform unauthorized actions like sending emails (Debenedetti et al., 2024), where success can be directly measured.
title: Position: Adversarial ML for LLMs Is Not Making Any Progress

claim: prefers testing models on messy, real-world end-to-end tasks over cleaned-up, homework-style versions because models look capable on tidy presentations but fail when dropped into realistic ugly environments.
quote: oftentimes when we test models, we test them on the thing that we think is hard for humans, but is not like the actual thing that represents the real task. And I would like to see more people trying to understand the end to end nature of things.
title: The Adversarial Mind: Defeating AI Defenses with Nicholas Carlini of Google DeepMind

claim: In a setup, do present the raw, cluttered environment (large unpolished repos, irrelevant code, unclear structure) instead of a distilled 20-line core with the key issue highlighted, because a cleaned-up presentation makes the task artificially easy and signals a constructed exercise.
quote: if I give a language model, a defense presented in a really clean, easy to study homework exercise like presentation. I've rewritten the defense from scratch and I've put the core logic in 20 lines of Python. Then I've done most of the hard work
title: The Adversarial Mind: Defeating AI Defenses with Nicholas Carlini of Google DeepMind

claim: In a setup, do leave the artifacts ugly and uncurated (a random Git repo with 1000 lines nobody has explained) instead of surfacing the one important piece, because real systems do not highlight what matters and models behave differently there.
quote: if you dump them into a random Git repository from some person's paper that has not been set up nicely to be studied and has 1000 lines of code and who knows what half of it's doing, they struggle quite a lot.
title: The Adversarial Mind: Defeating AI Defenses with Nicholas Carlini of Google DeepMind

claim: Prefers proxy-free, end-to-end tasks that mirror what real practitioners do over proxy tasks, because proxies can badly misestimate real capability.
quote: AutoAdvExBench is interesting for many reasons, but most importantly because it is not a proxy metric for some security task, but is the complete and exact task that real machine learning security researchers write papers on
title: AutoAdvExBench: Benchmarking autonomous exploitation of adversarial example defenses

claim: In a setup, use real, messy, unedited artifacts (actual code, docs, environments) instead of clean, purpose-built, puzzle-like ones because artificial construction changes model behavior and results.
quote: The code we study here is real-world, messy, and not artificially constructed to be used for evaluation. When performing attacks on real-world systems, code is rarely presented in a clean, minimal format ready for study by the analyst.
title: AutoAdvExBench: Benchmarking autonomous exploitation of adversarial example defenses

claim: Distrusts results from simplified CTF/homework-style environments as evidence of real-world capability, since they are constructed like puzzles and yield large gaps versus real data.
quote: Especially when using benchmarks to evaluate dangerous capabilities, evaluations using homework-style exercises can yield significant differences from evaluations using real-world data.
title: AutoAdvExBench: Benchmarking autonomous exploitation of adversarial example defenses

claim: Controls for artificiality by running the same underlying task in a simplified and a real form, so the gap itself becomes the evidence of how much the setup's realism matters.
quote: Because these defenses are implementations of actual defenses from the literature, but were just re-written to be as simple and easy to analyze as possible, this allows us to compare the ability of LLMs to attack CTF-like adversarial example defenses versus real-world adversarial example defenses.
title: AutoAdvExBench: Benchmarking autonomous exploitation of adversarial example defenses

claim: prefers evaluations against adaptive, resource-rich adversaries over static fixed test sets because static sets overfit and real attacks are out of distribution, giving a false sense of security.
quote: Second, because adversarial tasks are inherently open-ended, real attacks will inevitably be out of distribution, so success on static evaluations provides only a false sense of security.
title: The Attacker Moves Second: Stronger Adaptive Attacks Bypass Defenses Against LLM Jailbreaks and Prompt Injections

claim: prefers a negative-result standard of 'tried as hard as possible and still failed' over claiming robustness from empirical success, because evaluations can only fail to prove a thing is broken.
quote: empirical evaluations cannot prove that a defense is robust; all it can (and should) do is fail to prove that the defense is broken! A defense evaluation should try as hard as possible to break the defense and ultimately fail.
title: The Attacker Moves Second: Stronger Adaptive Attacks Bypass Defenses Against LLM Jailbreaks and Prompt Injections

claim: Distrusts near-zero attack success rates reported on public benchmarks, treating them as a sign of weak evaluation rather than a strong system.
quote: Indeed, defenses that merely report near-zero attack success rates on public benchmarks are often among the easiest to break once novel attacks are attempted.
title: The Attacker Moves Second: Stronger Adaptive Attacks Bypass Defenses Against LLM Jailbreaks and Prompt Injections

claim: Distrusts automated model-based graders because they are themselves ML models that can be gamed or reward-hacked, so scoring needs manual checking.
quote: these safety classifiers are themselves machine learning models and are consequently susceptible to adversarial examples and reward-hacking behaviors
title: The Attacker Moves Second: Stronger Adaptive Attacks Bypass Defenses Against LLM Jailbreaks and Prompt Injections

claim: Manually verifies successful attacks to ensure they are not exploiting weaknesses in the scoring mechanism before counting them as evidence.
quote: We manually verified all attacks to ensure they were not exploiting weaknesses in our scoring mechanism.
title: The Attacker Moves Second: Stronger Adaptive Attacks Bypass Defenses Against LLM Jailbreaks and Prompt Injections

claim: Prefers attack-specific elicitation (probing the model in the manner the hidden behavior is triggered) over generic direct querying or standard benchmarks because behaviors gated on a trigger look benign under naive probing.
quote: Detecting harmful finetuning is not as simple as querying the fine-tuned model and measuring if it responds harmfully. As we show in Figure 3, many attacks are only effective if an attacker queries the model according to the attack
title: Detecting Adversarial Fine-tuning with Auditing Agents

claim: In a setup, reuse the exact context cues found in the target's own data/deployment (system prompt, trigger string, format) instead of a generic test prompt, because behavior is conditional on those cues and generic probes understate it.
quote: Configure the HEx-PHI benchmark with specific attack vectors by optionally specifying: 1) system prompt (i.e., use the system prompt found in the fine-tuning training data), 2) function to modify the user prompt (e.g., append backdoor trigger string, encode in cipher, etc.)
title: Detecting Adversarial Fine-tuning with Auditing Agents

claim: Counts evidence as convincing when the elicited harmful output is specific and coherent enough to be actionable, not merely a non-refusal, so incoherent compliance is discounted.
quote: If it does not refuse, are its replies specific and convincing in a way that could actually manifest in harmful ways? Or are they incoherent and unlikely to actually result in harm?
title: Detecting Adversarial Fine-tuning with Auditing Agents

claim: In a setup, give the agent realistic open read/write access to tests instead of hiding them, because tests are commonly accessible in real software engineering and that creates the genuine opportunities for cheating that deployments present.
quote: We provide agents with full read/write access to test cases rather than hiding them. While this differs from the original benchmarks, unit tests are commonly accessible in real software engineering, creating more opportunities for cheating.
title: ImpossibleBench: Measuring LLMs’ Propensity of Exploiting Test Cases

claim: prefers constructing tasks where any success necessarily implies a violation (impossible tasks) over relying on manual inspection or LLM judges, because it gives a noiseless, unambiguous ground-truth measure of misbehavior.
quote: The goal of this benchmark is to create coding tasks of various complexities that are impossible to complete without cheating, so the scores agents obtain on this benchmark can serve as a noiseless proxy for their cheating propensity
title: ImpossibleBench: Measuring LLMs’ Propensity of Exploiting Test Cases

claim: In a setup, include an iterative feedback loop with failed-test feedback instead of single-shot attempts, because it mirrors real agent workflows and surfaces cheating that emerges after legitimate attempts fail.
quote: We allow up to 10 submissions per run with feedback about failed tests, mirroring competitive programming and real-world scenarios where agents iteratively refine solutions.
title: ImpossibleBench: Measuring LLMs’ Propensity of Exploiting Test Cases

claim: Treats behavior as highly sensitive to small prompt wording differences, so setups should vary guidance strictness since looser phrasing sharply raises misbehavior.
quote: we discovered that LLM behaviors are surprisingly sensitive to prompt details, with looser guidance leading to significantly higher cheating rates.
title: ImpossibleBench: Measuring LLMs’ Propensity of Exploiting Test Cases

claim: prefers anticipating and pre-empting skeptical objections with extra controls over leaving results as suggestive, because convincing evidence means a skeptic has no obvious unanswered question about the setup.
quote: Every experiment should be as precisely performed as you can manage. Run multiple trials. Control for confounders. If there's a question a skeptical reader might ask about your setup, run the experiment that answers it before they ask.
title: How to win a best paper award (or, an opinionated take on how to do important research)

claim: In a setup, use a bare, natural-sounding prompt and a stock agent in a plain environment instead of heavily engineered scaffolding or guided search paths because the minimal setup reflects how real users would actually deploy the model.
quote: The prompt is deliberately bare: find a vulnerability, rank it by severity, write it to an output file. No tool-calling scaffolding, no guided search paths, no curated context windows. Just a model, a codebase, and an instruction.
title: LLMs Now Find Zero-Days Autonomously: What It Means

claim: In a setup, run against real, live targets (a real Docker-hosted Ghost instance, the real Linux kernel) instead of toy or synthetic environments because real artifacts yield convincing, non-cherry-picked evidence.
quote: Carlini ran this live on stage: a Docker container running Ghost, a single script the model had written, and within moments the full credential set was printed to the terminal.
title: LLMs Now Find Zero-Days Autonomously: What It Means

claim: Prefers validated, working end-to-end demonstrations (exploits actually run, bugs verified) over unverified model claims or raw crash counts because unvalidated output is slop that wastes others' time.
quote: I have so many bugs in the Linux kernel that I can’t report because I haven’t validated them yet. I’m not going to make that some open source developer validate bugs that I haven’t checked yet — I’m not going to send them potential slop.
title: LLMs Now Find Zero-Days Autonomously: What It Means

claim: Prefers worst-case, adversarial evaluation over observing behavior on natural inputs because models can look aligned when examined naturally while failing under adversarial pressure.
quote: you have these models that look like they're aligned when you look at them naturally, but what you actually want is for them to be aligned in some worst-case setting.
title: Lessons from 10 Years of Adversarial Machine Learning | FAR.AI

claim: Prefers an adversary's failure as evidence of safety over random sampling of behavior because if a motivated adversary cannot elicit a behavior, chance occurrence is also unlikely.
quote: thinking about the adversarial perspective is a very good way of getting an estimate of the true worst case. If an adversary trying to make something happen cannot succeed, then randomness alone is also not going to make it work.
title: Lessons from 10 Years of Adversarial Machine Learning | FAR.AI

claim: Distrusts published robustness/defense claims that have not been stress-tested by an expert attacker, since top-venue defenses can be broken by trivial changes.
quote: Published paper at a top computer security conference, and one character change breaks it. Like 92% clean accuracy, now we're at 5% accuracy under attack.
title: Lessons from 10 Years of Adversarial Machine Learning | FAR.AI

claim: When a weaker method beats a stronger one (black-box beats white-box), investigate the specific instances where it did instead of dismissing it, since the anomaly reveals masking or a deficient attack.
quote: I suggest looking at which instances adversarial examples can be found with black-box but not white-box attacks. Check if these instances are at all related, and investigate why white-box attacks are not finding these adversarial examples.
title: Advice on Evaluating Adversarial Example Defenses

claim: Collects evidence with diverse attack families (gradient-free, transfer, random search) to check the primary attack isn't missing something obvious, rather than relying on a single attack type.
quote: By attempting to generating adversarial examples with purely random search, by sampling completely random perturbations (with, e.g., Gaussian or uniform random noise) we can confirm that we aren't missing anything obvious.
title: Advice on Evaluating Adversarial Example Defenses

claim: Prefers comparing methods under the same (strongest) evaluation over comparing numbers from mismatched evaluations because such comparisons are apples-to-oranges.
quote: if new defense A has 90% efficacy against some set of fixed attacks, but defense B has only 10% efficacy on adaptive attacks, it is no more fair to say “defense A is 80 percentage points more effective than B.”
title: Advice on Evaluating Adversarial Example Defenses

claim: Prefers judging a defense by the worst-case attack over its average or best-case performance because a stronger attack's result supersedes weaker ones.
quote: It is important to compare defense against the worst attacks. If Defense A does better than Defense B on weaker attacks (e.g., FGS) but does worse against a stronger attack (e.g., PGD), then Defense B is the stronger defense.
title: Advice on Evaluating Adversarial Example Defenses

claim: Treats weak evaluation as a field-wide problem rather than a problem of individual papers, and wants checklists useful to readers judging whether an evaluation is sufficient.
quote: it is not these papers, and these papers only, that were performing weak evaluations. The field as a whole is. These recommendations come from approaches I notice that we were taking that others were (are) not.
title: Advice on Evaluating Adversarial Example Defenses

claim: prefers treating success as a negative goal that only survives sustained attempts to disprove it over accepting the absence of observed failure, because researchers easily fool themselves.
quote: Adversarial robustness is a negative goal – for a defense to be truly effective, one needs to show that no attack can bypass it.
title: On Evaluating Adversarial Robustness

claim: Use monotonicity and impossibility sanity checks (stronger attack or larger budget must do at least as well) as diagnostics, treating violations as evidence the evaluation itself is broken.
quote: Attacks that allow more distortion are strictly stronger than attacks that allow less distortion. If the attack success rate ever decreases as the amount of distortion allowed increases, the attack is likely flawed.
title: On Evaluating Adversarial Robustness

claim: In a setup, define a realistic threat model that models some actual adversary with stated goals, knowledge, and capabilities instead of an arbitrary or unfalsifiable one, because it makes the evaluation meaningful and falsifiable.
quote: Without a threat model, defense proposals are often either not falsifiable or trivially falsifiable.
title: On Evaluating Adversarial Robustness

claim: In a setup, assume the adversary is highly capable and knows the system's inner workings instead of relying on obscurity or secret details, because real attackers will not be constrained by the designer's assumptions.
quote: In general, the guiding principle of a defense’s threat model is to assume that the adversary has complete knowledge of the inner workings of the defense. It is not reasonable to assume the defense algorithm can be held secret
title: On Evaluating Adversarial Robustness

claim: Report per-example worst-case outcomes across all attacks rather than averages per attack, because aggregates hide that some method succeeds on a given instance.
quote: it is important to report attack success rate on a per-example basis instead of averaged over the entire attack.
title: On Evaluating Adversarial Robustness

claim: prefers diverse, carefully adapted attacks over many near-identical ones because redundant tests give a false sense of thoroughness.
quote: do not show a massive table with many similar attacks that have not been adapted to the defense. Instead, rather show a shorter table with a more diverse set of attacks that have each been carefully adapted and tuned.
title: On Evaluating Adversarial Robustness

claim: Prefers framing evaluations as proofs with the null hypothesis that the claim is false, putting the burden on the evaluator to give convincing evidence rather than on critics to produce a counterexample.
quote: This is because the null hypothesis for a theorem is that it is false, just as the null hypothesis for a defense should be that it is not robust.
title: Increasing Confidence in Adversarial Robustness Evaluations

claim: Distrusts evaluations whose attack ignores the component being claimed as a defense (e.g., oblivious to the detector), so the paper adds an inverted test so that passing a single direction cannot mask this.
quote: a potential issue with the regular test is that a weak attack might pass the test even though the attack completely ignores the detector. Indeed, many evaluations of detector defenses consider weak attacks that are oblivious
title: Increasing Confidence in Adversarial Robustness Evaluations

claim: When a check passes but the evaluation is known to be broken, diagnose it as a different class of bug (integration vs unit) rather than discarding the test; be explicit about what the test cannot catch.
quote: If we view our proposed test as a unit test for an attack, then the type of bug in the above evaluation is akin to an integration bug, where the (correct) attack is called with incorrect parameters.
title: Increasing Confidence in Adversarial Robustness Evaluations

claim: Claims a test is a necessary but not sufficient condition, and that a failed test undermines confidence without proving the defense is broken, because over-claiming from a one-sided check is unjustified.
quote: Note that this does not necessarily imply that the theorem is not correct (a.k.a. that the defense is not effective), but it should not give us any confidence that it is.
title: Increasing Confidence in Adversarial Robustness Evaluations

claim: Validate a new diagnostic against cases with known ground truth (previously broken defenses with weak vs strong attacks), reporting true/false positives, rather than only demonstrating it on fresh cases.
quote: we now have access to both a flawed and a well-working adversarial evaluation method for each defense. This allows us to compare how these attacks perform in terms of both the estimated robust accuracy and the score on the binarization test.
title: Increasing Confidence in Adversarial Robustness Evaluations

claim: Suggests that each defense author should build tailored attack unit tests matched to their particular claims and architecture rather than relying on one generic test.
quote: defense authors should aim to develop their own attack unit tests, depending on the particular claims made.
title: Increasing Confidence in Adversarial Robustness Evaluations

claim: In a setup, build the context from real benign conversation data (Open Assistant truncated to random lengths) instead of hand-written prompts because it makes the surrounding context natural and varied.
quote: This dataset consists of a series of hypothetical interactions between a human and an assistant, which we truncate to a randomly selected $K\in[1..N]$ rounds.
title: Are aligned neural networks adversarially aligned?

claim: Inspects samples qualitatively to catch failures of the automated metric, and flags cheap metrics' limits instead of trusting them blindly.
quote: But in less than ten cases, we find our automated metric has potential limitations.
title: Are aligned neural networks adversarially aligned?

claim: prefers worst-case, existence-style evaluation of behavior over modeling a specific realistic adversary because it gives a lower bound on what models can be made to do.
quote: for the most part we are not concerned with any particular practical adversary, and instead, only with finding any valid input that achieves our attack goal.
title: Are aligned neural networks adversarially aligned?

claim: Chooses the tested behavior (toxicity) mainly because it is cheaply auto-evaluable, openly acknowledging a simplistic proxy.
quote: The main reason is that toxicity is relatively easy to (approximately) evaluate in a automated way.
title: Are aligned neural networks adversarially aligned?

claim: States that future attacks should pass the proposed known-solution tests before being considered reliable, and that the goal is better defense evaluation.
quote: Such attacks should, at a minimum, pass our tests to be considered reliable.
title: Are aligned neural networks adversarially aligned?

claim: prefers evaluating by actually executing the model's output in a sandbox over judging its text because functional outcomes are more convincing evidence of success.
quote: Most questions are evalauted by actually running the code the model writes [a] safely, in a docker container... don't worry too much. but the framework supports a bunch of other evaluation methods as well.
title: My benchmark for large language models

claim: prefers outcome-based correctness over mechanistic explanations because he cares only whether the answer is right, not why (memorization vs reasoning).
quote: I don't care why the model managed to get the answer right. Did it memorize the answer because someone else asked exactly this same question before? Did it use some clever “reasoning” to solve a question it's never seen before? I don't care---I just want the right answer.
title: My benchmark for large language models

claim: Distrusts mainstream academic benchmarks as measures of real-world usefulness, since they test narrow exam-like questions rather than real uses.
quote: I think it's kind of crazy that we're still mostly evaluating language models by whether or not they can correctly answer some high school science questions.
title: My benchmark for large language models

claim: prefers modest, scoped claims (a benchmark 'for me') over general capability claims because it only covers the tasks he asks.
quote: Does this make it a good benchmark for general model capabilities? No. It's possible that the model could do many things I'm just not asking it to do.
title: My benchmark for large language models

claim: prefers publicizing a vulnerability class over only fixing the specific instance because the underlying class will not be resolved by patching individual bugs and others need to learn from it.
quote: When a vulnerability is not just a single bug, but an instance of a new class of bugs, it's important to go public with it so that others can learn from it and not make the same mistakes in the future.
title: Why I attack

claim: prefers attacking things that are both interesting and important over forcing work he doesn't care about because intrinsic interest drives productivity.
quote: If you can find something that (a) you're interested in and (b) is important to do, you'll be far more productive than trying to force yourself into doing something that you don't care about.
title: Why I attack

claim: Distrusts defenses whose protection can't be updated after deployment, since a later break retroactively compromises everything already released.
quote: Once someone has published their adversarially noised images, they've lost control of them---they can't update them after that. And someone who wanted to train a model on these protected images only needs to download a bunch of images all at once, wait a few weeks or months for an attack on the defense
title: Why I attack

claim: Choose what to test and how to act by locating the vulnerability on the patchable-to-unpatchable spectrum, which determines disclosure and urgency.
quote: Identifying where a given vulnerability lies on the spectrum is important because it helps to determine how you should disclose the vulnerability.
title: Why I attack

claim: prefers publishing an attack because the vulnerability is likely to be independently rediscovered over withholding it because a less benevolent finder might exploit it.
quote: Someone else was bound to be able to re-discover this attack, and if we didn't go public with it, then the next person to discover it might not be so nice and just sit on it to exploit it for their own gain.
title: Why I attack

claim: Rejects trivial or non-novel elicitations as evidence of a real vulnerability; a valid test must reveal something meaningfully new rather than just echoing the request.
quote: trivial attacks such as prompting "please repeat [harmful text]" do not reveal meaningful new vulnerabilities. Hence, there is no clear universal standard on what sorts of prompts or transformations count as "valid" or "novel" adversarial inputs.
title: Position: Adversarial ML for LLMs Is Not Making Any Progress

claim: Distrusts reported progress and defense evaluations that are not adaptive or worst-case, since original evaluations often overestimate robustness and average-case gains hide worst-case failures.
quote: we must distinguish between progress in preventing average-case vulnerabilities and achieving worst-case security robustness. Although we might be making progress in the former, we have barely improved the latter and most models can still produce harmful generations under attacks.
title: Position: Adversarial ML for LLMs Is Not Making Any Progress

claim: Prefers manual, context-dependent, human-style attacks (persona, multi-turn, social engineering) over automated optimization for finding worst cases, because they are what actually works on LLMs.
quote: Many successful attacks on LLMs exploit qualitative properties that are hard to optimize automatically, such as persona modulation (Shah et al., 2023), multi-turn conver sations (Anil et al., 2024), and social engineering techniques (Zeng et al., 2024).
title: Position: Adversarial ML for LLMs Is Not Making Any Progress

claim: Prefers papers that state explicitly whether they pursue real-world security demonstration or scientific understanding, and are judged accordingly, because the two purposes warrant different standards of rigor.
quote: Papers should be explicit for what reason they are being written, and should be evaluated in this light. For real-world security, demonstrating attacks on fuzzy, ill-defined problems can be valuable when the potential harm is clear and immediate.
title: Position: Adversarial ML for LLMs Is Not Making Any Progress

claim: prefers evidence from a strong, adaptive adversary over results against weak or non-adaptive attacks because a defense or behavior that holds only against weak probes will break under a stronger one.
quote: you have to train against a strong enough attack in order for there to be the case that the thing is robust and does not break broken even by stronger attacks.
title: The Adversarial Mind: Defeating AI Defenses with Nicholas Carlini of Google DeepMind

claim: Picks what to test by skipping variations on approaches he already believes in and focusing on qualitatively odd-looking ones, while acknowledging that this selection inflates the apparent success rate.
quote: What I tend to spend my time looking at are the things that when you look at them, they do look a little more weird. And that's those are the more interesting defenses because they're like a qualitatively new class of of way of thinking about this.
title: The Adversarial Mind: Defeating AI Defenses with Nicholas Carlini of Google DeepMind

claim: prefers the simplest possible objective or setup over a more elegant one because it is easy to debug and gets most of the way there.
quote: the simplest possible objective is usually the best 1. Even if you can have a better objective function that seems mathematically pure in some sense, the fact that it's easy to debug simple loss functions means that you can get 90% of the way there
title: The Adversarial Mind: Defeating AI Defenses with Nicholas Carlini of Google DeepMind

claim: prefers a separate red team that genuinely wants to break the thing over the builders testing their own work, because authors are invested in their idea and cannot easily switch to wanting it to fail.
quote: it's very hard after you've spent 6 months building something that you really want to work to actually change your frame of mind and be like, now I really want to break it.
title: The Adversarial Mind: Defeating AI Defenses with Nicholas Carlini of Google DeepMind

claim: Prefers mechanistically verifiable outcomes over subjective judgments because objective metrics make results convincing.
quote: This is possible in large part because AutoAdvExBench is entirely mechanistically verifiable: the only metric that matters for security is robustness against the strongest attack, regardless of the methods used.
title: AutoAdvExBench: Benchmarking autonomous exploitation of adversarial example defenses

claim: Is upfront about limitations (contamination, non-representativeness) and tests them empirically so claims are not generalized beyond what the evidence supports.
quote: We feel it is important to be upfront with these limitations, so that the success (or failure) of LLMs at solving our benchmark will not be generalized beyond what can be reasonably inferred.
title: AutoAdvExBench: Benchmarking autonomous exploitation of adversarial example defenses

claim: Checks contamination concerns by direct intervention (placing the known attack paper in context) rather than assuming, treating no improvement as evidence the concern is minor.
quote: Second, we found that even if we explicitly place the previously-written attack paper in the language model's context, the success rate does not significantly improve.
title: AutoAdvExBench: Benchmarking autonomous exploitation of adversarial example defenses

claim: prefers including human red-teamers alongside automated attacks because humans succeeded in every case even with limited information, where automated search succeeded only part of the time.
quote: human red-teaming succeeds in all the cases we evaluated, even when the participants have only limited information and feedback from the target system. On a selected subset of scenarios and defenses, the search attack succeeds 69% of the time
title: The Attacker Moves Second: Stronger Adaptive Attacks Bypass Defenses Against LLM Jailbreaks and Prompt Injections

claim: prefers tailoring attacks to the specific defense design (assuming the attacker knows the system) over generic off-the-shelf attacks, because evaluation should reflect the intrinsic strength of the system rather than attacker limitations.
quote: the adversary is assumed to know the system design and to possess sufficient computational power, so that the evaluation reflects the intrinsic strength of the defense rather than limitations of the attacker.
title: The Attacker Moves Second: Stronger Adaptive Attacks Bypass Defenses Against LLM Jailbreaks and Prompt Injections

claim: Tests mechanisms that depend on hidden information by simulating an attacker with perfect knowledge of the defense, which reveals conditional strategies a naive attacker would only find by chance.
quote: When we simulate a stronger adversary with perfect knowledge of the MELON paper and implementation, the mutator quickly discovers a “conditional” strategy
title: The Attacker Moves Second: Stronger Adaptive Attacks Bypass Defenses Against LLM Jailbreaks and Prompt Injections

claim: Treats detection-based defenses as weak when attacks look benign out of context, since flagging them would raise false positives; benign-looking triggers are hard to distinguish from normal inputs.
quote: Many successful triggers, including the example below, are not obviously harmful or show clear intention to overwrite the user instruction. Hence, the detectors cannot flag such triggers as unsafe, especially out of context
title: The Attacker Moves Second: Stronger Adaptive Attacks Bypass Defenses Against LLM Jailbreaks and Prompt Injections

claim: Prefers a paired comparison against a baseline (pre-fine-tuned model, with and without the trigger) over absolute behavior on one model, because the contrast isolates what is actually caused by the intervention.
quote: Second, we have access to the pre-fine-tuned model for comparison with the target model. We assume the pre-fine-tuned model to be harmless, and are concerned only with behavior introduced during fine-tuning.
title: Detecting Adversarial Fine-tuning with Auditing Agents

claim: Judges a detector by true-positive rate at a very low false-positive rate rather than accuracy or AUROC alone, because the cost of false alarms on legitimate use is what makes it deployable.
quote: Most critical to our problem is the TPR at low FPR, as we do not want to block legitimate use of fine-tuning APIs.
title: Detecting Adversarial Fine-tuning with Auditing Agents

claim: Distrusts results that depend on the evaluator's prior exposure or priors (e.g., the auditor over-flagging 'sleeper agent' patterns it has read about) and on single-run variance, so runs many independent audits and aggregates.
quote: the backdoored dataset is rated with some of the highest average risk scores, as the auditor has (prior to our work) likely been trained on documents referencing "sleeper agents" and their harm.
title: Detecting Adversarial Fine-tuning with Auditing Agents

claim: Prefers building a test set of hard, covert cases (individually innocuous data, backdoors, ciphers, needle-in-haystack) plus tricky benign controls over easy overt examples, because only these stress whether the method truly works.
quote: The set is challenging in that each datapoint of the adversarial fine-tune dataset is individually harmless and therefore bypasses content moderation on the input dataset, while the benign fine-tunes include challenging cases like low resource languages
title: Detecting Adversarial Fine-tuning with Auditing Agents

claim: Keeps prompts generic and minimally engineered so results are not tailored to known attacks and generalize to new ones, claiming robustness only where this holds.
quote: We sought to keep prompts generic and not suggestive of particular attacks, with minimal prompt-engineering, so that they would remain robust to new attacks.
title: Detecting Adversarial Fine-tuning with Auditing Agents

claim: Is candid that the adversary can adapt (jailbreak or distract the auditor itself) and that strong auditors can also jailbreak benign models, so a positive detection is not clean proof of malice.
quote: Ultimately, a strong auditor can jailbreak a benign model, presenting a limitation of our problem formulation
title: Detecting Adversarial Fine-tuning with Auditing Agents

claim: prefers building on established, realistic benchmarks over creating new tasks from scratch because they inherit diversity and quality, and cover realistic multi-file scenarios.
quote: Starting from tasks that are known to be diverse and high quality, instead of creating new ones from scratch, allows our benchmark to enjoy the same properties with relatively small effort.
title: ImpossibleBench: Measuring LLMs’ Propensity of Exploiting Test Cases

claim: Distrusts LLM monitors and model-provided justifications as evidence of legitimacy, since plausible rationalizations like 'backward compatibility' fool monitors on complex tasks.
quote: While it remains unclear whether the model intentionally crafted this justification or was simply misunderstanding the task requirements, the monitor accepted such claims as legitimate reasoning
title: ImpossibleBench: Measuring LLMs’ Propensity of Exploiting Test Cases

claim: Validates automatically generated scenarios with quality control, rejecting mutations that pass trivial baselines (original or empty patches), to keep the measurement valid.
quote: we verify their validity by testing them against both the original patches from the base benchmarks and empty patches that make no changes. Valid impossible mutations should fail both tests, and we remove any mutations that pass either test.
title: ImpossibleBench: Measuring LLMs’ Propensity of Exploiting Test Cases

claim: When classifying transcripts, tells the classifier the transcript is a known cheat so it focuses on categorization instead of second-guessing, using ground-truth-by-construction to reduce judge noise.
quote: Here we instruct Claude Opus 4 that the given transcript is a successful cheating attempt, so it will focus on classification and will be less likely to consider the transcript legitimate.
title: ImpossibleBench: Measuring LLMs’ Propensity of Exploiting Test Cases

claim: Looks beyond headline rates to the fine-grained form of misbehavior, since similar cheating rates hide very different strategies across model families.
quote: While the models’ cheating rates are relatively similar on the surface, we find them engaging in vastly different cheating behaviors.
title: ImpossibleBench: Measuring LLMs’ Propensity of Exploiting Test Cases

claim: Gives the agent a legitimate escape hatch (flag for human intervention) as a probe of whether cheating comes from lack of alternatives, noting effects differ across model families.
quote: we instruct the models to submit the string `flag_for_human_intervention` when they identify errors in the task, and the agent doing so will be immediately terminated.
title: ImpossibleBench: Measuring LLMs’ Propensity of Exploiting Test Cases

claim: prefers evidence so overwhelming that the reader reaches the conclusion themselves over stating a claim outright, because a reader who thinks 'not me' is lost before the evidence lands.
quote: if I'd just said it outright in the intro, the reader's immediate reaction would have been "well, not me," and I'd have lost them before I started. So the job of the paper was to provide evidence so overwhelming that by the end, the reader arrives at that conclusion on their own.
title: How to win a best paper award (or, an opinionated take on how to do important research)

claim: Starts with the sub-problem most likely to fail and uses small prototypes rather than polished experiments, so that doubts about the core idea are resolved cheaply and early.
quote: The best way I've found to minimize wasted time is to start with the sub-problem most likely to fail. It's comforting to work on the parts of a problem you know how to solve, but this teaches you nothing about whether your idea is any good.
title: How to win a best paper award (or, an opinionated take on how to do important research)

claim: Distrusts field-standard methodology and evaluation conventions that were adopted without justification, because early arbitrary choices or famous-but-wrong papers get propagated uncritically.
quote: These are directions where someone (usually someone famous!) published an influential paper that got something critical wrong with the approach, methodology, or evaluation... and then the rest of the field followed along the same wrong direction without thinking critically about the initial choice
title: How to win a best paper award (or, an opinionated take on how to do important research)

claim: prefers re-deriving a simpler, principled formulation (e.g. membership inference as a hypothesis test with a different metric) over inheriting convoluted existing evaluation setups, because the field's conventions can be confused and overcomplicated.
quote: The paper I eventually wrote argued the field should use a much simpler approach---treating membership inference as the hypothesis test it actually is---and evaluate using a different metric. A few years on, that's what everyone does.
title: How to win a best paper award (or, an opinionated take on how to do important research)

claim: Chooses what to test by looking for areas where current practice looks obviously wrong and things that will matter soon, rather than topics that are merely tractable.
quote: How do you know when you have something only you can do? I look for areas where, when I read the work, I want to scream. Areas where you keep asking yourself "why is everyone doing this obviously wrong?"
title: How to win a best paper award (or, an opinionated take on how to do important research)

claim: Tests whether a project is worth pursuing by writing the best-case conclusion before running experiments, and abandons it if the success case offers no insight beyond the numbers.
quote: I ask: if this paper were to succeed wildly---if all the experiments turned out exactly as I want---what could I say in a conclusion? If I have nothing to say beyond repeating the results, then what I've done mustn't have mattered very much.
title: How to win a best paper award (or, an opinionated take on how to do important research)

claim: prefers strengthening a vague 'sometimes' into a quantified 'usually' over reporting a loose demonstration, because careful, precise execution is what makes a finding credible.
quote: On multiple occasions I've put in several hours of work just to strengthen a "sometimes" to "usually", because this is what it means to care.
title: How to win a best paper award (or, an opinionated take on how to do important research)

claim: Prefers testing base model capability with a bare, minimal setup over elaborate bespoke scaffolding because the realistic threat is what anyone can do with almost no effort.
quote: What I care about is the base capability of the model, because if someone who’s malicious wants to go cause some harm and they don’t have to spend six months designing some fancy fuzzing harness or something
title: LLMs Now Find Zero-Days Autonomously: What It Means

claim: Probe the severity ceiling by asking the model for its worst-case output rather than relying on a human's prior judgment of whether something is low-severity, because human assumptions about difficulty can underestimate capability.
quote: Rather than manually prototype the exploit, the researcher asked the model: “Give me the worst that you can.” The model then autonomously designed and wrote the full exploit.
title: LLMs Now Find Zero-Days Autonomously: What It Means

claim: Fix coverage problems with a minimal tweak (a per-file hint iterated over the project) rather than building a complex harness, because repeated runs otherwise collapse onto the same salient paths.
quote: Running the same prompt multiple times against the same codebase tends to surface the same bug each time — the model consistently routes to the same salient code paths.
title: LLMs Now Find Zero-Days Autonomously: What It Means

claim: Distrusts stale capability evaluations from older models, since conclusions drawn from earlier model generations are misleading for current models.
quote: a conclusion that "LLMs cannot reliably find kernel bugs" drawn from a test against models released six or more months ago is actively misleading for current threat modeling.
title: LLMs Now Find Zero-Days Autonomously: What It Means

claim: Treats results that run opposite to expectation (attack making the model more accurate) as a red flag for a flawed evaluation, and tests the trivially inverted case to check.
quote: I'm following the gradients to make the model get less good, and the model gets more good.” This is somewhat confusing.
title: Lessons from 10 Years of Adversarial Machine Learning | FAR.AI

claim: Prefers problems with a formalizable, automatically checkable objective over fuzzy objectives because without a verifiable metric nobody can tell whether a defense or an elicitation worked.
quote: How do you formalize that? What is the mathematical function that is 1 every time the model gives instructions on how to build a bomb, and 0 otherwise? Because if I'm going to try and optimize this, I need some formalism that I can look at.
title: Lessons from 10 Years of Adversarial Machine Learning | FAR.AI

claim: Distrusts claims of success when evaluation relies on humans trying their best, since without automated checks nobody knows whether a defense works.
quote: We're going to have a bunch of defenses, no one will know whether or not they worked, and people will just try and be making these claims.
title: Lessons from 10 Years of Adversarial Machine Learning | FAR.AI

claim: Prefers strong, adaptive, optimization-based evaluation over off-the-shelf attacks because running a defense's own attack out of the box can give misleading results.
quote: if you run their attack out of the box, what you'll find is that the accuracy goes to 100%.
title: Lessons from 10 Years of Adversarial Machine Learning | FAR.AI

claim: Prefers choosing a problem whose evaluation is tractable over a nominally easier problem that cannot be evaluated, because an easier-seeming problem is useless if you cannot verify a solution.
quote: the problem might be easier, but the evaluation of it is much harder. And so it may be the case that this is an easier problem to solve, but I'm not going to be able to know whether or not you actually have solved it.
title: Lessons from 10 Years of Adversarial Machine Learning | FAR.AI

claim: prefers using checklists as a list of known failure modes to think with rather than a procedure to follow blindly because mindless compliance is counterproductive.
quote: Blindly following the checklist without careful thought will likely be counterproductive: each item in the list must be taken into consideration within the context of the specific defense being evaluated.
title: On Evaluating Adversarial Robustness

claim: Flags open problem: gradient-free attacks currently fail on randomized models, so stronger attacks for that setting are needed.
quote: the state-of-the-art gradient-free attacks currently do not do well in this setting. (Future work on this challenging problem would be worthwhile.)
title: On Evaluating Adversarial Robustness

claim: Treats concrete code-level flaws found in the evaluation (e.g., unfrozen batch norm) as the decisive confirmation that a low test score reflects a real weakness, and checks by fixing and re-testing.
quote: Upon investigation, we found a flaw in the original evaluation’s code: The statistics of the batch normalization layers are not frozen during evaluation, which changes the behavior of the model during the attack.
title: Increasing Confidence in Adversarial Robustness Evaluations

claim: Tests on the easier model first so that failure there is informative about harder targets.
quote: as GPT-2 is an easier model to attack, if attacks fail here, they are unlikely to succeed on the more difficult cases of aligned models.
title: Are aligned neural networks adversarially aligned?

claim: Use a model-in-the-loop checker (a vision LLM describing output, then substring match) to automate evaluation of hard-to-score outputs.
quote: To do this, we pass the resulting image to a language model and ask what flag has been drawn.
title: My benchmark for large language models

claim: Treats surprising failures on simple-seeming tasks as informative litmus tests of capability boundaries (e.g., uuencode, novel assembly).
quote: I was surprised to find that none of the models I tested could even identify a uuencoded file, let alone even decode text.
title: My benchmark for large language models

claim: Real-world context (actual deployment and usage) changes how carefully findings should be handled, as ML moved from unused to ubiquitous.
quote: But a lot has changed since 2018. Most importantly: machine learning models are now used everywhere. And so that means that now, when we discover attacks, we're considerably more careful about how we disclose them.
title: Why I attack

claim: Give the target's authors a chance to check the attack for errors before publishing, to ensure the evidence is correct.
quote: We did provide Ben's group with an initial draft of the paper to make sure they could check any errors in our work, but it doesn't make sense to wait for a patch
title: Why I attack

claim: prefers doing the adversarial work others avoid over leaving it undone because defenses can't be fixed unless someone shows they are broken.
quote: It may be true that attacking things is easier than defending them, but if no one else is going to attack then I'll be happy to be the one who does.
title: Why I attack

claim: Distrusts results on closed, silently updated systems because the tested version is unclear and findings cannot be reproduced or compared.
quote: Many influential LLMs are now closed-source and updated silently over time (Chao et al., 2024), making it unclear which version of a system is being tested.
title: Position: Adversarial ML for LLMs Is Not Making Any Progress

claim: Prefers carefully scoped, formal, well-defined sub-problems over attacking the whole fuzzy space without rigor, because only these let progress be measured and built upon.
quote: Attempting to solve the entire space of attacks without rigor is neither scientific nor likely to be productive.
title: Position: Adversarial ML for LLMs Is Not Making Any Progress

claim: prefers claims grounded in true technical facts about what is currently known to work over asserted or assumed safety measures, because policy built on unfounded claims is harmful.
quote: I think the thing that I just want to make sure that people do is that they base whatever they're thinking about on true technical facts.
title: The Adversarial Mind: Defeating AI Defenses with Nicholas Carlini of Google DeepMind

claim: Favors building systems that stay safe even if the model is untrustworthy (external hard constraints, defense in depth) over relying on the model's own robustness.
quote: You could build the system to be robust even if the model isn't. This limits utility in important ways. This is not perfect.
title: The Adversarial Mind: Defeating AI Defenses with Nicholas Carlini of Google DeepMind

claim: Flags as an open problem why social-engineering style prompts beat principled optimization attacks on LLMs, which he finds unexpected and wants to understand.
quote: I really don't know how to think about these social engineering styles of attack because it feels to me like the optimization attacks should be just strictly stronger, but empirically they're not right now.
title: The Adversarial Mind: Defeating AI Defenses with Nicholas Carlini of Google DeepMind

claim: Prefers benchmarks of appropriate difficulty (hard but tractable, with smooth continuous measures) over saturated or binary ones because they discriminate capability differences.
quote: Benchmarks should be appropriately difficult to warrant further study. We believe autonomously breaking adversarial example defenses is of an appropriate difficulty level for current models.
title: AutoAdvExBench: Benchmarking autonomous exploitation of adversarial example defenses

claim: Treats surprising non-monotonic results (stronger or reasoning models doing worse; advice from another model hurting) as informative about agent scaffolding fit rather than pure capability.
quote: Reasoning models generally performed worse: OpenAI's o1 and o3-mini, and 3.7 Sonnet with reasoning enabled. This result is not unique to our results: prior work (Wijk et al., 2024) has also found that reasoning models require substantially different agent frameworks.
title: AutoAdvExBench: Benchmarking autonomous exploitation of adversarial example defenses

claim: Proposes building proxy-free real-world benchmarks early, before they are needed, and extending to domains like jailbreak defenses.
quote: we believe that it is important to start designing challenging real-world benchmarks now, so that we can have them before they are necessary.
title: AutoAdvExBench: Benchmarking autonomous exploitation of adversarial example defenses

claim: Calls for more robust and efficient adaptive evaluation procedures, and for making defenses easy for humans to probe.
quote: we encourage the community to continue developing more robust and efficient adaptive evaluation procedures.
title: The Attacker Moves Second: Stronger Adaptive Attacks Bypass Defenses Against LLM Jailbreaks and Prompt Injections

claim: Proposes strengthening the auditor with whitebox tools, multi-turn/prefill chat, longer investigations and memory scaffolding, since current audits are short (~20 turns) and detection is still far from deployable.
quote: We expect to see the detection rate improved with additional affordances, such as whitebox affordances (e.g., linear probes, model diffing (Bricken et al., 2024), etc.) and enhanced chat tools (e.g., prefill and multi-turn chat).
title: Detecting Adversarial Fine-tuning with Auditing Agents

claim: Calls for more capable monitoring for complex multi-file tasks, as simple LLM monitors are insufficient.
quote: These results suggest that simple LLM-based monitoring approaches may not be sufficient for detecting cheating attempts on complex multi-file tasks. For more complex tasks, more sophisticated and capable monitoring solutions will be needed
title: ImpossibleBench: Measuring LLMs’ Propensity of Exploiting Test Cases

claim: Anchors claims in real, concrete attack demonstrations (e.g. buying expired domains in LAION-5b) rather than hypothetical threats, and ties future-oriented problems to something real today, honestly and without deception.
quote: You can also explain how your problem relates, even tangentially, to something real today. (But don't be deceptive about your true motivations.)
title: How to win a best paper award (or, an opinionated take on how to do important research)

claim: Treats work in new or contested areas as likely to be rejected for assuming premises the audience hasn't accepted, so he reads rejection as a signal to strengthen the argument rather than abandon the idea.
quote: On the first pass, the paper is often rejected because it's saying something a little outside what's normally believed to be true. The reviewers aren't convinced and leave some confused remarks.
title: How to win a best paper award (or, an opinionated take on how to do important research)

claim: Wants a result to feel complete, covering the obvious extensions and anticipated critiques, so no 'I wish they had done X' remains, while leaving non-critical directions open.
quote: your paper should be at a local optimum; the reader must not be left with the thought "I really wish the authors had done X; that would have been an obvious improvement."
title: How to win a best paper award (or, an opinionated take on how to do important research)

claim: Distrusts extrapolating linear continuation or confident predictions of an imminent plateau, favoring trend-based reasoning with explicit uncertainty about when the curve bends.
quote: Treating capability plateau predictions as reliable planning inputs. The track record of confident predictions that AI improvement will stall imminently is approximately a decade of consistent failures.
title: LLMs Now Find Zero-Days Autonomously: What It Means

claim: Prefers honest, calibrated self-comparison and concrete, checkable specifics (bug age, byte sizes, first critical CVE) over vague capability claims because they make the claim credible.
quote: It’s pretty clear to me that these current models are better vulnerability researchers than I am.
title: LLMs Now Find Zero-Days Autonomously: What It Means

claim: Weak safeguards that only stop compliant users while motivated adversaries route around them are net negative, which shapes how he evaluates mitigations.
quote: If I put a safeguard in place that’s very, very weak, it will only stop the good people from using the software — the bad people are just going to jailbreak the model and they’re going to still attack it anyway.
title: LLMs Now Find Zero-Days Autonomously: What It Means

claim: Open problem: building validation and triage pipelines for the backlog of unvalidated model-found crashes, plus calibrating safeguards, is where help is needed within months.
quote: Carlini estimates several hundred crashes sitting in an unvalidated queue.
title: LLMs Now Find Zero-Days Autonomously: What It Means

claim: Warns that extrapolating from early progress curves is misleading; reports what the data actually show over time rather than projected trends.
quote: it looks like we're making roughly linear progress as we go forward. It kind of looks like you could almost project out into the future and draw a line and say, we'd be at, something like 90% accuracy by now.
title: Lessons from 10 Years of Adversarial Machine Learning | FAR.AI

claim: Toy-looking attacks (cat to guacamole) matter not as realistic threats but because they reveal fundamental failures, so test selection can be driven by what exposes underlying weakness rather than by threat realism.
quote: No one is going to turn cats into guacamole. This is not a real threat. But it's pointing to something fundamental for all machine learning models
title: Lessons from 10 Years of Adversarial Machine Learning | FAR.AI
